Consult Summary:
- Telehealth consult for 2–3 days of new shortness of breath with wheeze and cough in a person with known asthma; poor relief from salbutamol; plan made for short-term inhaler escalation and urgent in-person review. Differential considerations include acute asthma exacerbation and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Shortness of breath with wheeze and cough; noted first during a run 2–3 days ago.
- Course/timeline: Symptoms began 2–3 days ago; now occurs with brisk walking. No improvement with blue inhaler.
- Exertional relationship: Initially during running; persists with brisk walking.
- Medications tried: Salbutamol (blue inhaler) used as needed and sometimes prophylactically; patient reports minimal benefit.
- Associated symptoms: Wheeze, cough.
- Sputum: Denies sputum production.
- Triggers/exposures: Not specified.
- Prior asthma control: Last attack 3–4 years ago; asthma generally controlled until past 2–3 days.
- Monitoring: No current peak flow done; patient-reported “when well” peak flow approximately 380 (units not specified) per recall.
- Allergic/atopic history: Hay fever; possible eczema (patient suspects).
- Family atopy: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Safety concerns discussed: If breathing worsens while awaiting review—attend Emergency Department.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma
  - No prior hospital admissions for asthma.
  - Never used oral steroids.
  - Last asthma review ~2 years ago.
- Hay fever (allergic rhinitis).
- Possible eczema (patient suspects; not confirmed).

Medications:
- Salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed; currently using daily and sometimes prophylactically; dose/puff count not documented.
- Clenil (beclomethasone, “brown” inhaler) preventer twice daily prior to this consult; specific prior puff count unclear. Plan: increase to 4 puffs twice daily.
- Cetraben (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Hydrocortisone (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: No known drug allergies. Environmental: hay fever.

Social History:
- Physically active (running).
- Smoking, alcohol, and substance use: Not discussed.

Family History:
- Brother: Asthma.
- Sister: Eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (telehealth visit).

Investigations:
- None obtained during this visit.
- Plan for in-person: Chest examination and peak flow measurement.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Probable acute loss of asthma control with mild exacerbation over 2–3 days, characterized by wheeze, cough, and exertional dyspnea with suboptimal response to reliever. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction may be contributing.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Acute asthma exacerbation (high): Known asthma, new wheeze/cough/dyspnea, increased reliever use with limited relief; no sputum.
  - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (medium): Onset with running and persists with brisk walking; more likely a contributor given ongoing symptoms.
  - Viral URI triggering asthma (low–medium): Acute onset with cough; no fever or systemic symptoms reported.

- Issue 1: Acute shortness of breath/wheeze—probable asthma exacerbation
  - Plan:
    - Increase Clenil (brown inhaler) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
    - Continue salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed, up to every 2–4 hours; frequent need indicates poor control.
    - Arrange face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest exam and peak flow measurement.
    - Depending on in-person findings, may require antibiotics and/or oral steroids (to be decided at review).
    - Safety net: If breathing worsens before the appointment, go to the Emergency Department (A&E).

- Issue 2: Asthma care gap (no review for ~2 years)
  - Plan:
    - Book in-person asthma review (GP/asthma nurse) for assessment, peak flow, and overall management update.

- Issue 3: Atopy (hay fever) and possible eczema
  - Plan:
    - No changes discussed today; continue current skin treatments as previously used (specifics not reviewed in this consult).

- General plan items:
  - Monitor symptoms and reliever use while awaiting appointment.
  - Attend urgent care/ED if deterioration occurs despite above measures.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: No vitals; no physical exam; no current peak flow recorded; smoking status not documented; medication doses/routes/frequencies incompletely documented (salbutamol puff count; cetraben/hydrocortisone details).
- Conflicts: None between transcript and DDx noted. Eczema diagnosis uncertain (patient suspects; not confirmed).
- Transcript quality: Occasional unclear medication naming initially (e.g., “Flanel/Bactroban” later clarified to Cetraben and hydrocortisone).
